questions.stem: A 78 year old woman has been bed-bound on a stroke ward for 10 days. Her whole left leg is now swollen with pitting oedema to the thigh and dilated superficial veins over the shin. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The skin is intact.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged immobility plus unilateral whole-leg pitting oedema and dilated superficial (collateral) veins is a DVT until proven otherwise.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: bed-bound on a stroke ward for 10 days
whole left leg is now swollen
steps.x: Prolonged immobility is a provoking factor; unilateral swelling with collateral veins shows deep venous obstruction.

elim: Usually a spreading, well-demarcated erythema from a skin break, often with fever; it does not cause dilated superficial veins.
Chronic, non-pitting swelling developing over months, not acute after 10 days of immobility.
Causes sudden calf pain and swelling below the knee in someone with knee arthritis, not whole-leg oedema with collateral veins.
A tender cord along a superficial vein without whole-leg swelling.

steps.x: **B. Deep vein thrombosis.** Immobility + unilateral swollen leg + collateral veins = DVT.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 2 day history of an aching, heavy right calf. She had an emergency caesarean section 12 days ago. Her right calf measures 4 cm more than the left and is tender along the deep veins. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her wound is clean.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The postpartum period and surgery are both VTE risk factors; a heavy, tender, swollen calf is DVT.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Postpartum plus recent surgery = strong VTE risk; unilateral calf swelling and deep vein tenderness.

elim: No injury or exertion, and strain does not cause 4 cm of swelling with deep vein tenderness.
No skin break, spreading erythema or fever.
Causes breathlessness and bilateral oedema from heart failure, not a single swollen calf.
Typical in knee arthritis with sudden pain behind the knee; postpartum state points to thrombosis.

steps.x: **C. Deep vein thrombosis.** Postpartum + unilateral tender swollen calf = DVT.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a left popliteal deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound. She has not travelled, had surgery or been immobile. She started a new medication 3 months ago for hot flushes and night sweats. She has hypertension controlled with amlodipine and osteoarthritis of the knees. Her BMI is 24 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor?
questions.e: Oestrogen (HRT or COCP) causes hypercoagulability and is a classic VTE risk factor.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: new medication 3 months ago for hot flushes and night sweats
steps.x: A recent drug for menopausal symptoms is HRT: oestrogen raises clotting factor levels.

elim: Calcium channel blockers cause ankle oedema but do not cause thrombosis.
An arterial risk factor, not a recognised cause of venous thrombosis.
Only relevant if it causes major immobility, which she does not have.
Age adds little on its own; the recent oestrogen exposure is the specific trigger.

steps.x: **B. Hormone replacement therapy.** Oestrogen therapy (HRT/COCP) is a VTE risk factor through hypercoagulability.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a right calf deep vein thrombosis after a 13-hour flight. Two days later he has sudden pain, pallor and coldness of his left arm. The left radial pulse is absent. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and regular, and his ECG shows sinus rhythm. A bubble study is arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
questions.e: A venous clot causing an arterial embolism (paradoxical embolism) needs a right-to-left shunt such as an atrial septal defect.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: sudden pain, pallor and coldness of his left arm
steps.x: A venous thrombus followed by an arterial embolus in sinus rhythm means the clot crossed the heart.

elim: Causes syncope and angina, but no route for a venous clot into the arterial system.
Not associated with paradoxical embolism.
Can embolise, but would not explain the timing just after a venous thrombosis.
Causes left atrial thrombus mainly with AF; his rhythm is sinus.

steps.x: **B. Atrial septal defect.** DVT + arterial embolus = paradoxical embolism through an ASD.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man had a left total knee replacement 6 days ago. His left calf became swollen yesterday. He now has sudden breathlessness and sharp right-sided chest pain on breathing in. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 104/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
questions.e: A DVT that embolises to the pulmonary arteries causes sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia; this needs emergency assessment.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Calf DVT, then pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest.

elim: Pain is pleuritic, and hypoxia with a clear chest after a swollen calf points to embolism.
Would give fever, cough and focal crackles; his chest is clear.
No trauma or line insertion, and breath sounds are not reported as absent.
He has not collapsed and is hypoxic and tachycardic.

steps.x: **C. Pulmonary embolism.** DVT + sudden breathlessness and hypoxia = PE, an emergency.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a second deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. The first was 2 years ago with no trigger. His mother had a pulmonary embolism at 35 and his uncle had a DVT at 40. He does not smoke, has not travelled and takes no medication. Examination is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Recurrent, unprovoked DVT in a young patient with a family history should prompt thrombophilia assessment; factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: His mother had a pulmonary embolism at 35
steps.x: Young, recurrent, unprovoked, with first-degree relatives affected: an inherited hypercoagulable state.

elim: A bleeding disorder, not a cause of thrombosis.
Causes low platelets and bleeding, not recurrent clots.
Rare at 24 and would usually show a raised haemoglobin or itch; strong family history points to an inherited cause.
An inherited bleeding disorder, the opposite of what he has.

steps.x: **A. Factor V Leiden.** Young + recurrent unprovoked VTE + family history = thrombophilia (factor V Leiden).

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a 3 day history of pain in his right calf. He drove a lorry for 14 hours a day for the last week. His temperature is 37.2°C and pulse rate 84 bpm. His right calf feels warm and tense. A deep vein thrombosis is suspected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Calf swelling 3 cm greater than the left
questions.e: Unilateral calf swelling of 3 cm or more compared with the other side is a classic DVT sign and scores on the Wells score.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Prolonged sitting gives venous stasis; a warm, tense calf suggests DVT.

elim: An arterial sign; DVT does not occlude arterial flow.
Bilateral oedema suggests heart failure, hypoalbuminaemia or drugs, not a unilateral DVT.
A sign of chronic venous insufficiency, not an acute DVT.
Typical of cellulitis or erysipelas.

steps.x: **C. Calf swelling 3 cm greater than the left.** DVT sign: unilateral calf swelling ≥3 cm (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity).

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen left leg. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg and her urine shows no protein. Her left calf is red, warm and 4 cm larger than the right. Her right leg is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state; a unilateral red, hot, swollen leg (often the left) is DVT.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: red, warm and 4 cm larger than the right
steps.x: Pregnancy is a VTE risk factor; swelling is one-sided and inflamed.

elim: No skin break, fever or spreading erythema; the asymmetric swelling points to a clot.
Bilateral, painless and symmetrical, not one red, painful leg.
Needs raised BP and proteinuria; both are normal.
Unlikely in a healthy young woman without knee disease.

steps.x: **B. Deep vein thrombosis.** Pregnancy + unilateral red, hot, swollen leg = DVT.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man is having chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer. He has a 4 day history of his whole right leg becoming swollen and heavy. He is afebrile. The leg has pitting oedema to the groin and is tender along the femoral vein. His left leg is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Active cancer is a major VTE risk factor (and a Wells item); whole-leg swelling with deep vein tenderness is DVT.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Active cancer, whole leg swollen and deep vein tenderness: three Wells items.

elim: Would cause bilateral, symmetrical oedema.
Develops slowly and is not tender along the femoral vein.
Causes severe pain, systemic toxicity and fever; he is afebrile and well.
Causes bilateral oedema with a raised JVP.

steps.x: **B. Deep vein thrombosis.** Active cancer + unilateral whole-leg swelling = DVT.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has a left femoral deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound after a 16-hour flight. He is reluctant to take tablets and asks what could happen if he goes home without treatment. He is otherwise well with normal observations.
questions.q: Which is the most serious complication he is at risk of in the coming days?
questions.e: An untreated proximal DVT can propagate and embolise to the lungs; PE is the major life-threatening complication.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Proximal (femoral) clots are most likely to embolise; the question asks about the short term.

elim: Rare with a DVT and not the main danger.
A long-term complication over months to years, and not life-threatening.
Not an acute or dangerous complication.
A late result of chronic venous hypertension.

steps.x: **C. Pulmonary embolism.** The danger of DVT is embolisation as a PE.

questions.stem: A 42 year old builder knocked his right shin on scaffolding 10 days ago and has rested at home since. He now has an aching, heavy right calf that is worse on walking. His temperature is 37.1°C. The calf is swollen, warm and tender deep in the muscle. There is no bruising and the knee is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Minor trauma plus immobility are transient provoking factors; a heavy, warm, tender, swollen calf is DVT.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Minor trauma and immobility provoke clots; the calf signs fit DVT.

elim: Develops within hours of major trauma with severe pain on passive stretch, not 10 days later.
Would follow a direct calf injury with bruising; there is none.
No skin wound, spreading erythema or fever.
His knee is normal.

steps.x: **D. Deep vein thrombosis.** Minor trauma + immobility + swollen tender calf = provoked DVT.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman had a left ischaemic stroke 2 days after a deep vein thrombosis of her right calf. She has had breathlessness on exercise for years. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on cardiac auscultation?
o: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound
questions.e: Paradoxical embolism after DVT points to an atrial septal defect, which gives fixed splitting of S2 and often RBBB.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: ischaemic stroke 2 days after a deep vein thrombosis
steps.x: DVT then stroke in sinus rhythm = paradoxical embolism; RBBB and years of exertional breathlessness suggest an ASD.

elim: Aortic stenosis; it does not allow a venous clot into the arterial system.
Mitral stenosis, which causes left atrial clots mostly in AF.
Mitral regurgitation; no right-to-left shunt.
A sign of heart failure, not of a shunt.

steps.x: **B. Fixed splitting of the second heart sound.** ASD: fixed split S2, RBBB, paradoxical embolism from a DVT.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has been recovering at home from pneumonia and has barely left his chair for 2 weeks. His left calf is now tight and aching. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His left calf is swollen and tender. A deep vein thrombosis is suspected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Bilateral pitting oedema to the knees
Painless hard lump in the popliteal fossa
White, cold leg with reduced sensation
questions.e: Deep venous obstruction diverts blood into collateral superficial veins, a sign that scores on the Wells score.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: barely left his chair for 2 weeks
steps.x: Immobility and a tight, aching calf: DVT. Look for signs of deep venous obstruction.

elim: An arterial finding; DVT does not block arterial inflow.
Bilateral oedema suggests a systemic cause such as heart failure.
Suggests a popliteal aneurysm or cyst, not DVT.
An acutely ischaemic limb, an arterial emergency.

steps.x: **C. Dilated non-varicose superficial veins.** DVT signs: swelling, pitting oedema, tenderness and collateral superficial veins.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a deep vein thrombosis of the right leg with no provoking factor. She has had three miscarriages before 10 weeks. She takes no medication. Investigations show a normal full blood count and a prolonged APTT that does not correct with mixing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: An unprovoked DVT in a young woman with recurrent miscarriage and a lupus anticoagulant (APTT not correcting) is antiphospholipid syndrome, an acquired thrombophilia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Unprovoked DVT in a young patient should prompt a search for thrombophilia; miscarriage plus lupus anticoagulant is the pattern.

elim: A prolonged APTT here would correct with mixing and cause bleeding, not clots.
A haemolytic anaemia; her blood count is normal.
Causes low platelets; her count is normal.
A bleeding disorder.

steps.x: **A. Antiphospholipid syndrome.** Unprovoked DVT + recurrent miscarriage = antiphospholipid syndrome.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 2 day history of a swollen left calf. She had a laparoscopic hysterectomy 2 weeks ago. Her left calf is 3.5 cm larger than the right, with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins. Her 2-level Wells score is 3. It is 10 am and the ultrasound department is open.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours
Start warfarin and review in clinic
questions.e: A Wells score of 2 or more means 'DVT likely': arrange a proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Wells ≥2 = DVT likely; imaging is available now.

elim: She has no chest symptoms; it does not image the leg veins.
With 'DVT likely' a negative D-dimer cannot rule out DVT; she needs imaging.
Delaying assessment risks propagation and PE.
Warfarin alone is not the diagnostic pathway; imaging comes first.

steps.x: **C. Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours.** Wells ≥2: ultrasound within 4 hours.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a swollen right calf after a 12-hour flight. It is 9 pm on a Saturday. His right calf is 4 cm larger than the left and tender along the deep veins. His 2-level Wells score is 2. He has no bleeding risk and normal renal function. Ultrasound will not be available until Monday morning.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Discharge with no treatment until the scan
questions.e: If 'DVT likely' and ultrasound cannot be done within 4 hours, give interim anticoagulation with a DOAC and take a D-dimer, then scan as soon as possible.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.

clues: not be available until Monday morning
steps.x: Likely DVT but the scan is delayed beyond 4 hours.

elim: Aspirin is not adequate anticoagulation for suspected DVT.
Not the standard pathway; NICE advises interim anticoagulation and ultrasound.
Leaves a likely DVT untreated for 36 hours.
Reserved for massive PE or limb-threatening DVT, not routine DVT.

steps.x: **D. Interim apixaban and a D-dimer.** Scan delayed >4 hours: interim DOAC plus D-dimer, scan within 24 hours if possible.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 2 day history of mild aching in her left calf after a long walk. Her 2-level Wells score is 0. Her calves are the same size and there is no tenderness along the deep veins. A D-dimer is negative.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: DVT excluded; consider an alternative diagnosis
questions.e: With Wells ≤1, D-dimer is the best initial test; a negative result rules DVT out.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Low probability and negative D-dimer.

elim: Not needed: a negative D-dimer in a low-risk patient rules DVT out.
No benefit once DVT is excluded.
No DVT has been shown.
Interim anticoagulation is for 'DVT likely' with delayed imaging.

steps.x: **A. DVT excluded; consider an alternative diagnosis.** Wells ≤1 + negative D-dimer = DVT excluded.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen left calf. Her left calf is 3 cm larger than the right and tender. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. She has no chest symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: In pregnancy, suspected DVT is investigated with compression duplex ultrasound.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Pregnant, leg symptoms only.

elim: Uses ionising radiation and contrast; ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy.
Rises normally in pregnancy so cannot reliably rule out DVT.
Not first-line; reserved for suspected pelvic vein thrombosis.
A test for PE, and she has no chest symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Compression duplex ultrasound.** Pregnant + suspected DVT = compression duplex ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has a 3 day history of a swollen left leg. His whole left leg is swollen and there is tenderness along the deep veins. His calves are 2 cm different. He has not been immobilised in a cast and has no superficial collateral veins. His 2-level Wells score is calculated (see item resources).

visual.title: 2-level Wells score for DVT
visual.label: Score 3
visual.caption: Score of 2 or more: 'DVT likely', so arrange ultrasound within 4 hours.

questions.q: Which is his 2-level Wells score?
questions.e: Active cancer, whole leg swollen and deep vein tenderness score 1 each = 3, so 'DVT likely'.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Count each Wells item: cancer 1, whole leg 1, tenderness 1; calf difference under 3 cm scores 0.

elim: He has three positive features.
Active cancer alone would score 1, but there are two more items.
Misses one of the three positive items.
Calf swelling is only 2 cm, below the 3 cm threshold, so it does not score.

steps.x: **D. 3.** Wells ≥2 = DVT likely: ultrasound within 4 hours.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has a 4 day history of a swollen, painful right leg. She is having chemotherapy for ovarian cancer. Her right calf is 4 cm larger than the left with pitting oedema. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her 2-level Wells score is 4.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Compression ultrasound of the leg veins
questions.e: Compression (proximal leg vein) ultrasound is the gold-standard diagnostic test for DVT.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Active cancer and leg signs: DVT likely, so imaging is needed.

elim: Images the pulmonary arteries; she has no chest symptoms.
Raised by cancer and chemotherapy and cannot confirm DVT; with Wells ≥2 imaging is needed.
Not used to diagnose DVT.
Shows bone and joint disease, not vein thrombosis.

steps.x: **A. Compression ultrasound of the leg veins.** DVT is confirmed by compression ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man had suspected left leg deep vein thrombosis with a 2-level Wells score of 2. His D-dimer is raised. Proximal leg vein ultrasound today shows no thrombus. He is well, and his calf is less swollen. His interim rivaroxaban is stopped.
questions.q: When should the ultrasound be repeated?
questions.e: Wells 'likely', D-dimer positive but ultrasound negative: stop anticoagulation and repeat the scan in 1 week.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Positive D-dimer with a negative first scan.

elim: Too soon to detect a calf clot that has propagated.
Far too late to catch propagation of a missed clot.
Too late; the guideline repeat interval is shorter.
Not the recommended interval.

steps.x: **A. 1 week.** Negative scan + positive D-dimer: repeat ultrasound in 1 week.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a left femoral deep vein thrombosis with no provoking factor. For 3 months he has had looser stools and has lost 5 kg. He is pale. Investigations: haemoglobin 98 g/L (130–180) and MCV 71 fL (80–100).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate further investigation?
questions.e: An unprovoked DVT should prompt assessment for malignancy; change in bowel habit with iron deficiency anaemia needs colonoscopy.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Unprovoked DVT plus red flags for colorectal cancer.

elim: Looks for a shunt or heart disease; it will not explain weight loss and iron deficiency.
Assesses arterial disease, which he does not have.
The DVT is already confirmed.
His age, weight loss and anaemia point to cancer, not an inherited thrombophilia.

steps.x: **A. Colonoscopy.** Unprovoked DVT: look for an underlying cancer, guided by symptoms.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 1 day history of a mildly sore right calf. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her calves are the same size and there is no oedema or tenderness. Her 2-level Wells score is 0. A D-dimer is raised.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
questions.e: With Wells ≤1, a positive D-dimer cannot confirm DVT (low specificity), so proceed to proximal leg vein ultrasound.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Low probability but a positive D-dimer: DVT is not excluded.

elim: She has no chest symptoms.
A raised D-dimer means DVT has not been excluded.
Does not answer whether there is a clot now.
DVT must be confirmed or excluded first.

steps.x: **C. Proximal leg vein ultrasound.** Wells ≤1: D-dimer first; if positive, ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a right calf deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound. It developed 10 days after she sprained her ankle and rested it at home. She has no other risk factors and no bleeding risk. She is started on apixaban.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
questions.e: A DVT provoked by a transient non-surgical factor (minor trauma, immobility, travel) is treated for 3 months.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: sprained her ankle and rested it at home
steps.x: A transient, removable trigger: provoked DVT.

elim: Longer than needed for a clot provoked by a transient risk factor.
The duration for unprovoked or cancer-associated DVT.
Too short for a proximal or provoked DVT under current guidance.
For recurrent unprovoked VTE or antiphospholipid syndrome.

steps.x: **B. 3 months.** Provoked DVT: anticoagulate for 3 months.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with metastatic lung cancer has a left femoral deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound. He is not having chemotherapy that interacts with anticoagulants. His eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73m² and he has no bleeding history. His platelet count is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Active cancer-associated DVT is treated with a DOAC for 6 months.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Active cancer and no contraindication to a DOAC.

elim: Aspirin does not treat VTE.
Too short for cancer-associated thrombosis.
Only if anticoagulation is contraindicated.
Warfarin is less suitable in cancer and 3 months is too short.

steps.x: **C. DOAC for 6 months.** Cancer-associated DVT: DOAC for 6 months, then review.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman who is 18 weeks pregnant has a left femoral deep vein thrombosis confirmed on compression duplex ultrasound. Her weight is 72 kg, her renal function is normal and she has no bleeding history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Pregnancy is a special case where DOACs are unsuitable; treatment-dose LMWH is used.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Pregnancy rules out DOACs and warfarin.

elim: DOACs cross the placenta and are not used in pregnancy.
Not a treatment for established VTE.
DOACs are avoided in pregnancy.
Teratogenic and avoided in pregnancy.

steps.x: **C. Low molecular weight heparin.** DVT in pregnancy: LMWH.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has a proximal deep vein thrombosis. He has a mechanical mitral valve and already needs warfarin, which he stopped 2 weeks ago before dental surgery. Warfarin is to be restarted. His INR today is 1.0.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to start his anticoagulation?
o: LMWH for 24 hours then warfarin alone
LMWH with warfarin for at least 5 days and until INR 2–3
Warfarin alone, checking INR in 1 week
questions.e: When warfarin is used, LMWH is given at the same time for at least 5 days and until the INR is in range (2–3).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
DOACs are unsuitable, so the warfarin pathway is needed.

elim: DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.
Warfarin takes days to work and is initially prothrombotic; overlap must last at least 5 days.
Leaves him unprotected while INR rises.
Aspirin does not cover the early period and adds bleeding risk.

steps.x: **C. LMWH with warfarin for at least 5 days and until INR 2–3.** Warfarin pathway: overlap with LMWH ≥5 days and until INR 2–3.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with chronic kidney disease has a right femoral deep vein thrombosis. Her creatinine clearance is 12 mL/min. She is not on dialysis and has no bleeding history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
questions.e: Severe renal impairment is a special case where DOACs are unsuitable; use LMWH (dose-adjusted) or the warfarin pathway.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Severe renal impairment makes DOACs unsuitable.

elim: DOACs are unsuitable at creatinine clearance below 15 mL/min.
Does not treat VTE.
Renally excreted and contraindicated in severe renal impairment.
Avoided at creatinine clearance below 15 mL/min.

steps.x: **D. LMWH followed by warfarin.** DOAC unsuitable (severe CKD): LMWH or warfarin pathway.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man returns to the ward at 2 pm after an elective total hip replacement. There were no bleeding problems in theatre. An intermittent pneumatic compression device is fitted. His eGFR is 80 mL/min/1.73m². The team plans pharmacological VTE prophylaxis.
questions.q: When should prophylactic-dose LMWH first be given?
questions.e: Surgical VTE prophylaxis: intermittent pneumatic compression immediately, then prophylactic-dose LMWH from 12 hours post-op.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: intermittent pneumatic compression device is fitted
steps.x: Mechanical prophylaxis is already on; the question is when to add LMWH.

elim: Too early: risk of bleeding at the surgical site.
Not the post-operative timing advised.
Leaves him unprotected in the high-risk early period.
Prophylaxis starts while he is immobile, the period of highest risk.

steps.x: **B. 12 hours after surgery.** Post-op: IPC immediately, LMWH 12 hours after surgery.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a second deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Neither episode had a provoking factor. He completed 6 months of apixaban after the first, 2 years ago. Cancer has been excluded. He has no bleeding risk and is keen to avoid another clot.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
questions.e: Unprovoked DVT is treated for 6 months, and longer (often long term) if recurrent and bleeding risk is low.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: Neither episode had a provoking factor
steps.x: Recurrent, unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk.

elim: For a clot provoked by a transient risk factor.
He has already had recurrence after 6 months.
Too short.
Aspirin is much less effective than continued anticoagulation.

steps.x: **D. Long term, with regular review.** Unprovoked: 6 months; recurrent: continue long term.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman is in the emergency department with a left calf deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound. While waiting for her first dose of rivaroxaban, she becomes suddenly breathless and faint. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Elevate the leg and give analgesia
questions.e: Sudden breathlessness, collapse, tachycardia and hypoxia in a patient with DVT suggest PE and need emergency ABCDE assessment.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a left popliteal deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound after a 15-hour flight. He weighs 82 kg, his eGFR is 95 mL/min/1.73m², his platelet count is normal and he takes no other medicines. He has no bleeding history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: A DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban), a factor Xa inhibitor, is first-line for DVT when there is no contraindication.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Normal renal function and no special case: a DOAC.

Reserved for severe renal failure or when rapid reversal may be needed.
Needs LMWH cover and INR monitoring; DOACs are first line.

steps.x: **E. Rivaroxaban.** First-line DVT treatment: DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a left calf deep vein thrombosis. She has not travelled, had surgery or been immobile, and her veins have not been injured. Testing shows she is heterozygous for factor V Leiden, which makes factor Va resistant to inactivation by activated protein C.
questions.q: Which component of Virchow's triad explains her thrombosis?
questions.e: Thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden make blood hypercoagulable, one limb of Virchow's triad.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.

clues: not travelled, had surgery or been immobile
resistant to inactivation by activated protein C
steps.x: No stasis or injury; the abnormality is in clotting factors.

elim: No surgery, trauma or line has damaged her veins.
Raised viscosity is from excess red cells or protein, not factor V Leiden.
Factor V Leiden affects the coagulation cascade, not platelets.
She has been mobile and has not travelled.

steps.x: **B. Hypercoagulability.** Thrombophilia, malignancy, oestrogen and pregnancy = hypercoagulability.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man in intensive care has had a femoral central venous catheter for 9 days. His right leg becomes swollen and an ultrasound shows thrombus around the catheter in the femoral vein. He has no personal or family history of thrombosis and his blood count is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism initiating this thrombosis?
questions.e: An indwelling catheter damages the vein wall, exposing subendothelial tissue that activates clotting: endothelial injury in Virchow's triad.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
A foreign body inside the vein damages the endothelium.

elim: An inherited thrombophilia; no history suggests it.
His blood count, including platelets, is normal.
His blood count is normal.
Increased fibrinolysis breaks clots down; it does not cause them.

steps.x: **B. Endothelial injury.** Surgery, trauma and lines = endothelial injury.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man develops a deep vein thrombosis 4 days after an emergency laparotomy. Ultrasound shows that the thrombus began in a deep calf vein just above a venous valve and has extended into the popliteal vein. He asks why the clot started there.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: High arterial pressure damages calf veins
Platelet-rich thrombus forms at sites of fast flow
Slow flow in valve pockets activates coagulation
The calf veins have no valves
questions.e: DVT forms most often in deep calf or proximal leg veins, where slow flow and valve pockets favour activation of the coagulation cascade.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.

clues: began in a deep calf vein just above a venous valve
steps.x: The site is a venous valve pocket in the calf, where stasis is greatest.

elim: Relevant to atheroma, not venous thrombosis.
Veins are low-pressure; arterial pressure does not reach them.

steps.x: **D. Slow flow in valve pockets activates coagulation.** Venous thrombus starts where flow is slowest: valve pockets in the deep calf veins.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a left femoral deep vein thrombosis. Her left leg is swollen, warm, red and tender. A medical student asks why the leg is swollen when the clot is only in a vein.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is started on apixaban for a proximal deep vein thrombosis. He asks how the tablet stops the clot growing. The doctor explains that it binds directly to one activated clotting factor.

steps.x: **A. Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin.** DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) block factor Xa, so less thrombin is made.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman had an extensive right femoral deep vein thrombosis 3 years ago. She now has a heavy, aching right leg worse at the end of the day, ankle swelling, brown skin pigmentation and venous eczema. Ultrasound shows no new thrombus but reflux through the deep veins.
